greek: καὶ αὐτὰ δὲ τὰ νῦν αὐτῶν εἰρημένα συμπτώματα, πλὴν τῆς ἀχροίας, ἐγκέφαλόν τε καὶ στόμαχον [577] κατειληφότων ἐστίν· ἀγρυπνίαι μὲν γὰρ καὶ ὕπνοι διὰ τὸν ἐγκέφαλον, ὀρέξεις δὲ καὶ ἀνορεξίαι διὰ τὸν στόμαχον ἄλλοτε ἀλλοίως διατιθέμενον γίγνονται. δῆλον δ’ ὅτι τὸ στόμα τῆς γαστρὸς εἴρηται νῦν στόμαχος, ἐν ᾧ τὸ μὲν φλέγμα τὸ ἀθροισθὲν, ὡς ὀλίγον ἔμπροσθεν εἴρηται, τὰς ὀρέξεις ἐποίησε· τῶν δὲ χολωδῶν, ἐπὶ μὲν τῆς ξανθῆς διψώδεις τε καὶ ἀσώδεις ἔσονται, καὶ τὸ στόμα πικρὸν αὐτοῖς ἐστιν· ἐπὶ δὲ τῇ μελαίνῃ, δύσθυμοι, καὶ σκυθρωποὶ, καὶ φοβεροὶ, καὶ ἄδιψοι, καὶ σιέλου μεστοὶ, ἀπόσιτοι δὲ οὐ πάντες, ἀλλά τινες αὐτῶν. ἱκανῶς δὲ πεινώδεις εἰσὶν οἷς ἂν ἡ μέλαινα τὴν ὀξεῖαν ποιότητα κρατοῦσαν ἔχῃ· γίγνεται δὲ τοῦτο, κακοηθεστέρας αὐτῆς ἀποτελουμένης. ἔστ’ ἂν δὲ μόνον οἷον ἰλὺς αἵματος ᾖ, μήπω δ’ ἀκριβῶς ὀξεῖα, κάλλιον ἴσως (μελαγχολικὸς χυμὸς ἕως οὗ λέγεται) μηδὲ καλεῖν μηδέπω τὸν τοιοῦτον χυμὸν μέλαιναν χολὴν, ἀλλ’, ὥσπερ εἴωθα, μελαγχολικὸν, ὅτι τοῦ γενέσθαι μέλαιναν χολὴν πλησίον ἥκει.
rendering_1: And the very symptoms of them that have now been mentioned, apart from the bad colour, belong to them when they have occupied the brain and the stomachos [577]; for sleeplessness and sleep come about on account of the brain, while appetites and losses of appetite come about on account of the stomachos, which is disposed differently at different times. And it is clear that the mouth of the stomach has here been called stomachos, in which the phlegm that has gathered, as was said a little earlier, produced the appetites; but of the bilious humours, in the case of the yellow they will be thirsty and nauseous, and their mouth is bitter; whereas in the case of the black, they are despondent, sullen, fearful, without thirst, and full of saliva, but not all of them averse to food, only some of them. And those are considerably hungry in whom the black bile has the acid quality predominating; and this comes about when it is rendered more malignant. But so long as it is merely like a sediment of blood, and not yet precisely acid, it is perhaps better (so far as it is called a melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile either, but, as I am accustomed, melancholic, because it has come near to becoming black bile.
rendering_2: And these very symptoms of theirs just now stated, except for the loss of colour, belong to [humours] that have taken possession of the brain and the stomach [577]; for sleeplessness and sleep come about on account of the brain, and appetites and want of appetite on account of the stomach, as it is disposed now in one way, now in another. It is clear that by 'stomach' (stomachos) is now meant the mouth of the belly (gastēr), in which the phlegm that has collected, as was said a little before, produced the appetites. Of the bilious, those with yellow bile will be thirsty and nauseated, and their mouth is bitter; those with black bile are despondent, sullen, fearful, free of thirst and full of saliva; not all of them are averse to food, but some of them are. Those in whom the black [bile] has the sour quality predominating are considerably hungry; and this comes about when it is rendered more malignant. But so long as it is only like a sediment of blood, and not yet strictly sour, it is perhaps better (until it is called melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile at all, but, as I am accustomed, melancholic, because it has come close to becoming black bile.

greek: ἀλλ’ οὐ νῦν καιρὸς ὑπὲρ τῆς ἐν ταῖς κακοχυμίαις διεξέρχεσθαι διαφορᾶς, ὅτι μηδὲ πλῆθος εἶπον ὀνομάζεσθαι αὐτάς· ἡμῖν δὲ οὐχ ἁπλῶς τὸ πλεονάζον ὁπωσοῦν ἐξευρεῖν, ἀλλὰ περὶ πλήθους ﻿ [578] σκέψασθαι προὔκειτο· πλεονεξία δέ ἐστι τοῦτο τῶν καθ’ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ζώου χυμῶν. οὔτ’ οὖν τῶν κατὰ μέρος ὄγκων οὔτε κακοχυμίας ἀκούειν χρὴ ποθεῖν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷδε τὰς ἰδέας, ἀλλ’ ὅταν ἤτοι κατὰ τὴν ἀρχαίαν ἀναλογίαν αὐξηθῶσιν ἅπαντες, ἤ τινα βραχεῖαν ὑπεροχὴν ἐξ αὐτῶν εἷς λάβῃ. τὸ μὲν οὖν αἷμα παμπόλλην ὑπεροχὴν δύναται λαβεῖν ἐν ταῖς πληθωρικαῖς διαθέσεσι, τῶν δὲ ἄλλων χυμῶν οὐδείς· κακοχυμία γὰρ ἤδη τό γε τοιοῦτον, οὐκ ἔτι πλῆθος, οὐδὲ πληθώρα καλεῖται.
rendering_1: But now is not the occasion to go through the difference among the cacochymiai, since I said that they are not even called plethos; for our proposed task was not simply to discover what is in excess in whatever manner, but to inquire about plethos; [578] and this is an excess of the humours throughout the whole body of the animal. One ought not, then, to desire to hear in this discourse about the forms either of the local swellings or of cacochymia, but about when either all the humours are increased according to their original proportion, or one of them acquires some slight preponderance. Now blood can acquire a very great preponderance in the plethoric dispositions, but none of the other humours can; for such a thing is already cacochymia, and is no longer called plethos, nor plethora.
rendering_2: But this is not the time to go through the differences among the cacochymias, since I said that they are not even called plenitude. Our proposed task was not simply to find out whatever is in excess in any way whatsoever, but to examine plenitude [578]; and this is an excess of the humours throughout the whole body of the animal. So in this discourse one must not long to hear the kinds either of swellings in particular parts or of cacochymia, but only of the case when either all the humours have increased in their original proportion, or one of them has acquired some slight preponderance. Now blood can acquire a very great preponderance in plethoric conditions, but none of the other humours can; for such a thing is by then called cacochymia, and no longer plenitude or plethora.

greek: ἔναγχος γοῦν ἀγγεῖον κασσιτέρινον εἰς τοσοῦτον διεφυσήθη πρὸς τοῦ περιεχομένου κατ’ αὐτὸ φαρμάκου τοῦ διὰ τῶν ἐχιδνῶν, ὥστε καὶ τὸ περικείμενον αὐτῷ δέρμα καὶ τὸ σχοινίον ᾧ κατεδέδετο ῥαγῆναι καὶ [550] τὸ πῶμα κυρτωθῆναι. καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ ὅτι μεγίσταις ὀδύναις ἐνίοτε καταλαμβάνονταί τινες, ὑπὸ φυσώδους πνεύματος καταληφθέντος ἔν τισι τοῦ ζώου μέρεσι, καὶ ὡς ἕν τῷ κώλῳ μάλιστα συμβαίνειν εἴωθε τοῦτο, γινώσκειν ἡγοῦμαι πάντας, οἷς ἐπιμελές ἐστιν ἀκολουθεῖν τε καὶ διασκέπτεσθαι τὰ καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἐπὶ τῶν καμνόντων ὁρώ μενα. βέλτιον οὖν ὑπὸ πάσης οὐσίας ὑγρᾶς καὶ πνευματώδους εἰς τονώδη διάθεσιν ἄγεσθαι νομίζειν τὰ μόρια, ἢ μόνῳ τῶν χυμῶν αἵματι πληθύνοντι τοιοῦτον ἕπεσθαι πάθημα. μεταβῶμεν οὖν αὖθις πρὸς τοὺς ὡς πρὸς τὴν δύναμιν ἡγουμένους ἀεὶ συνίστασθαι τὸ πλῆθος, ἐρωτήσωμέν τε καὶ τούτους ἕν τι τῶν προχειροτάτων, ὑποθέμενοι τοιάνδε τινα ὑπόθεσιν, ὡς ἐπὶ παραδείγματι.
rendering_1: Recently, at any rate, a tin vessel was so greatly inflated by the drug contained in it, the one prepared from vipers, that both the leather wrapped around it and the cord with which it had been tied burst, and [550] the lid was bulged outward. And indeed that some people are at times seized by the greatest pains when flatulent pneuma has been trapped in certain parts of the animal, and that this is wont to happen especially in the colon, I think is known to all who take care to follow and examine what is seen every day in the case of the sick. It is better, therefore, to hold that the parts are brought into a tensive condition by every moist and pneumatic substance, than that such an affection follows upon blood alone among the humours when it increases in quantity. Let us pass again, then, to those who think that plethora is always constituted in relation to the faculty, and let us ask these too one of the most obvious questions, positing some such hypothesis as the following, by way of example.
rendering_2: Recently, at any rate, a tin vessel was so inflated by the drug contained in it, the one made from vipers, that both the skin placed around it and the cord with which it had been tied down burst, and [550] the lid was bulged outwards. Moreover, I think that all who take care to follow and examine what is seen day by day in patients know that some people are sometimes seized by very great pains when flatulent pneuma is trapped in certain parts of the animal, and that this is accustomed to happen most of all in the colon. It is better, then, to hold that the parts are brought into a tensive condition by every moist and pneumatic substance than that such an affection follows upon blood alone among the humours when it is in excess. Let us therefore pass over once more to those who think that plethora always arises in relation to the strength, and let us ask them too one of the most obvious things, positing a supposition of the following kind, by way of example.

greek: καὶ μὴν καὶ τρίτος τις ἄλλος ἐστὶ χορὸς, οὔτε γινώσκων, εἴτε ἔστιν, εἴτε οὐκ ἔστι τις δύναμις, οὔτε ζητεῖν ὁμολογῶν, ἀλλ’ ἐπί τισιν ἐναργῶς φαινομένοις σημείοις περὶ τὸν κάμνοντα συνισταμένοις, ἐκ πείρας μακρᾶς εὑρῆσθαι φάσκων ἑαυτῷ τὴν κένωσιν· εἶτ’ ἐρωτώμενος ἅττα ποτέ [516] ἐστι τὰ σημεῖα ταῦτα, διάτασιν ἀγγείων φησὶ, καὶ ἔρευθος καὶ βάρος ὅλου τοῦ σώματος, ὄκνον τε πρὸς τὰς κινήσεις καὶ τάσεις τῶν μελῶν. ἔνιοι δὲ αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν ἑλκώδη καὶ κοπώδη προστιθέασιν αἴσθησιν, ἀργόν τε τὸν ἔμπροσθεν βίον ἐν προσφοραῖς ἐδεσμάτων τε καὶ πομάτων πλείοσι, καὶ συνήθων ἐκκρίσεων ἐποχῇ. ἐπὶ ταύτῃ γοῦν τῇ συνδρομῇ, καλοῦσι γὰρ οὕτω τὸ ἄθροισμα τῶν συμπτωμάτων, τετηρῆσθαι φλεβοτομίαν ὠφελοῦσαν. οὗτοι μὲν οὖν οὐ μόνον ἑαυτοὺς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ἅπαντας ἀνθρώπους ἀφαιροῦνται τὸν λόγον, ἐκ πείρας εὑρῆσθαι πάντα φάσκοντες· οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι, καθάπερ εἴρηται νῦν δὴ, λόγῳ τε χρῆσθαί φασι, καὶ τὴν δύναμιν οἱ μὲν ὡς οὐδ’ ὅλως ἔστιν, οἱ δὲ ὡς ἔστι μὲν, ἥτις δ’ αὐτῆς ἡ οὐσία, μὴ γινώσκεσθαί φασιν· ὡς ὀλιγίστους εἶναι τοὺς ἀποφήνασθαι τολμῶντας ὕπαρξίν τε καὶ οὐσίαν δυνάμεως.
rendering_1: And indeed there is also a third, further band, which neither knows whether there is or is not some faculty, nor admits to inquiring into it, but asserts that, on the basis of certain clearly apparent signs which come together in the patient, the evacuation has been discovered by itself from long experience; then, when asked what exactly [516] these signs are, it says distension of the vessels, and redness and heaviness of the whole body, and reluctance toward movements, and tensions of the limbs. Some of them add also the ulcerous and lassitude-like sensation, and an idle previous manner of life amid rather abundant intakes of foods and drinks, and the suppression of customary excretions. Upon this syndrome, at any rate—for so they call the aggregate of symptoms—phlebotomy has been observed to be beneficial. These men, then, deprive not only themselves but also all other human beings of reason, asserting that everything has been discovered from experience; while the others, as has just now been said, say that they use reason, and as for the faculty, some say that it does not exist at all, others that it exists, but that what its substance is is not known; so that very few are those who dare to declare both the existence and the substance of a faculty.
rendering_2: And indeed there is also a third band, a different one, which neither knows whether there is or is not some faculty, nor agrees to inquire into it, but asserts that, upon certain signs that appear clearly and arise in the patient, evacuation has been found by it from long experience. Then, when asked what [516] these signs are, it says: distension of the vessels, and redness and heaviness of the whole body, sluggishness towards movements, and tensions of the limbs. Some of them also add the ulcerous and lassitude-like sensation, and an idle previous way of life with rather large intakes of foods and drinks, and retention of the habitual excretions. Upon this syndrome, at any rate (for so they call the aggregate of the symptoms), venesection has been observed to be beneficial. These people, then, deprive not only themselves but all other men as well of reason, asserting that everything has been found from experience. The others, as was said just now, say that they use reason, and concerning the faculty some say that it does not exist at all, others that it does exist but that what its substance is is not known. So those who dare to declare both the existence and the substance of a faculty are very few.

greek: οἱ σφυγμοὶ δὲ κατὰ τὰς δυσκρασίας τὰς ὀκτὼ τὴν ἰδέαν ἐκείνην ἕξουσιν, οἵαν ἐν τῇ τῶν σφυγμῶν πραγματείᾳ διήλθομεν· εἴτε δ’, ὡς εἵρηται, μόνου τοῦ αἵματός ἐστιν, εἴτε διά τινα ἐπιμιξίαν χυμοῦ, διορίζεσθαι χρὴ τῇ τε συνούσῃ χρόᾳ παντὸς τοῦ σώματος καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις συμπτώμασιν, ὅσα περὶ ὕπνου καὶ ἐγρηγόρσεως, ἢ ὀρέξεως καὶ ἀνορεξίας, ἢ εἴτι τοιοῦτον, μικρὸν ἔμπροσθεν εἴρηται, καὶ τῇ προηγησαμένῃ διαίτῃ, καὶ τοῖς γυμνασίοις, καὶ τοῖς αὐτῷ τῷ κάμνοντι συμπίπτειν εἰθισμένοις, ἔτι τε τῇ ὥρᾳ καὶ τῇ χώρᾳ καὶ τῇ φυσικῇ πυκνότητι καὶ ἀραιότητι τοῦ σώματος· ἄμεινον γὰρ ἐκ πάντων τὸ πιστὸν τῇ διαγνώσει λαμβάνειν, οὐκ ἐξ ἑνὸς ἢ δυοῖν, εὖ εἰδότας ὡς αὐτὸ μόνον ἐν τῇ [581] τέχνῃ πλεῖστα κεκοινώνηκε τοῦ στοχάζεσθαι, λέγω δὴ τὸ μέρος τῆς τέχνης τοῦτο τὸ διαγνωστικὸν ἅπαν, οὐ μόνον τὸ κατὰ τὴν κακοχυμίαν, ἢ τὸ πλῆθος, ἃ νῦν ἡμῖν διορίζεσθαι πρόκειται· τὰ γὰρ περὶ τὰς ἐνεργείας, ἢ τὰς τῶν νοσημάτων αἰτίας, ἢ τὰς ἰάσεις, ἐπιστημονικώτερον ἔχει τὴν γνῶσιν. εἴρηται δ’ ἐπὶ πλέον ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν τούτων ἑτέρωθι, καὶ νῦν ἀρκέσει τὸ προστεθὲν αὐτάρκως διορισαμένους, αὐτόθι που καταπαῦσαι τὸ γράμμα. γίγνοιτο δ’ ἂν αὐτάρκης ὁ λόγος ἐπὶ παραδείγματι ἐξετασθείς. ἔστω δὴ τὸν μὲν ἄνθρωπον ἀπύρεκτον ὑπάρχειν, ἐν ὄγκῳ δὲ μείζονι τὰς φλέβας αὐτῷ καὶ τὸ σύμπαν σῶμα ἐρυθρότερον.
rendering_1: The pulses, in accordance with the eight dyscrasias, will have that form which we went through in the treatise on the pulses; and whether, as has been said, it belongs to the blood alone, or is due to some admixture of a humour, one must distinguish by the colour accompanying the whole body and by the other symptoms—as many as have been mentioned a little earlier concerning sleep and wakefulness, or appetite and lack of appetite, or anything else of the kind—and by the regimen that has preceded, and the exercises, and the things that habitually befall the patient himself, and further by the season and the region and the natural density and rarity of the body; for it is better to take the assurance for the diagnosis from all of these, not from one or two, knowing well that this alone in the [581] art has the greatest share in conjecture—I mean this whole diagnostic part of the art, not only that which concerns cacochymia or plethos, which it is now our task to distinguish; for the matters concerning the activities, or the causes of diseases, or the cures, have a knowledge that is more scientific. These very matters have been discussed at greater length elsewhere, and now it will suffice, having adequately determined what has been added, to bring the treatise to a close at just about this point. And the account would become sufficient if examined on an example. Let it be supposed, then, that the man is free of fever, but that his veins are of greater volume and his whole body redder.
rendering_2: The pulses in the eight dyscrasias will have that form which we set out in the treatise on pulses. Whether, as has been said, it belongs to the blood alone, or arises from some admixture of a humour, one must determine by the accompanying colour of the whole body and by the other symptoms (those concerning sleep and waking, or appetite and lack of appetite, or anything of that kind, which were stated a little earlier), and by the preceding regimen, and the exercises, and the things that are accustomed to befall the patient himself, and further by the season and the country and the natural density and rarity of the body. For it is better to take the assurance for the diagnosis from all of these, not from one or two, knowing well that this alone in the [581] art has the largest share in conjecture: I mean this whole diagnostic part of the art, not only that which concerns cacochymia or plethora, which we now propose to distinguish. For matters concerning the functions, or the causes of diseases, or the cures, admit of a more scientific knowledge. More has been said about these very matters elsewhere, and for now it will suffice, once we have adequately determined what has been added, to bring the writing to a close somewhere about here. The account would become adequate if it were examined by way of an example. Let it be, then, that the man is without fever, but that his veins are of greater bulk and his whole body redder.

greek: ἀλλὰ οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἰατρῶν ὅμοιόν τι πεπόνθασι τῷ πρὸς Ἱπποκράτους εἰρημένῳ περὶ τῶν ἐπὶ κατάγμασιν ἢ τοιούτοις τισὶ παθήμασι τὰ προσταττόμενα μὴ ποιούντων· καὶ γὰρ κᾀκεῖνοι, καίτοι ὑγιεῖς ἐθέλοντες γενέσθαι, ﻿ [553] τὸν ἐν τῇ θεραπείᾳ κάματον οὐχ ὑπομένουσιν, ὥσπερ οὗτοι τὸν ἐν τῷ μανθάνειν. ἀλλ’ οὔτε ἐξαίφνης ὑγιεῖς οἷόν τε γενέσθαι μόνῳ τῷ βούλεσθαι τυχόντας τοῦ τέλους, οὔτε τούτους ἐπιστημονικοὺς, ἄνευ τοῦ διελθεῖν ἅπασαν τὴν ὁδὸν, ἣν ἀρτίως ἐδήλωσα. γνώσονται γὰρ, εἰ βουληθεῖεν, ὡς ἡ ἑλκώδης ὅλου τοῦ σώματος αἴσθησις, ἥ τε ἐπὶ πλέοσι γυμνασίοις ἀήθως παραληφθεῖσι γιγνομένη καὶ ἡ χωρὶς γυμνασίων ἄφνω συστᾶσα, δακνώδους ἔγγονος ὑπάρχει χυμοῦ. καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τοὺς πλέον γυμνασαμένους ἐλαίῳ τε πλείονι καὶ τρίψει μαλακῇ καὶ λουτροῖς γλυκέων ὑδάτων θερμοῖς ἀκριβῶς εὐκράτοις οἱ γυμνασταὶ θεραπεύουσιν, ὡς διαφορηθῆναι τοὺς δακνώδεις χυμοὺς, ὅσοι γυμνασαμένων ἀμετρότερον ἐγεννήθησαν ἐπὶ συντήξει πιμελῆς καὶ σαρκὸς μαλακῆς, ἢ δι’ αὐτοὺς τοὺς ἐν τῷ σώματι χυμοὺς ἰσχυρῶς θερμανθέντας.
rendering_1: But the majority of physicians have suffered something similar to what was said by Hippocrates concerning those who, in the case of fractures or some such affections, do not do what is prescribed; for those too, although they wish to become healthy, [553] do not endure the toil involved in the treatment, just as these do not endure the toil involved in learning. But it is not possible either for the former to become healthy all at once, attaining the end by the mere wishing, or for the latter to become scientific without traversing the whole road which I have just now set out. For they will come to know, if they should wish it, that the ulcerous sensation of the whole body, both that which arises upon more numerous exercises undertaken contrary to habit and that which forms suddenly without exercises, is the offspring of a biting humour. And for this reason the gymnastic trainers treat those who have exercised too much with more abundant oil and soft rubbing and warm baths of sweet waters that are precisely well-tempered, so that the biting humours may be dispersed—all those that were generated, when they exercised rather immoderately, upon the colliquation of fat and of soft flesh, or on account of the humours in the body themselves having been strongly heated.

greek: [541] πότερον ἄλλό τι σημαίνει τὸ εὐτονώτεροι τοῦ ἰσχυρότεροι, καὶ δύο ἡμᾶς ἐδίδαξε σημεῖα τοῦ μετρίου πλήθους, ἢ δύο μὲν εἰπὼν ὀνόματα, σημεῖον δὲ ἕν; ἐγὼ δὲ οὐδεμίαν εὑρίσκω τοῦ σημαινομένου διαφορὰν, οὔτε κατὰ τὸ γένος οὔτε κατὰ τὸ εἶδος οὔτε ἐν τῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἧττον, ἀλλ’ ὑφ’ ἑκατέρου σημαίνεσθαι νομίζω ταὐτόν. εἰ δὲ βούλει, τίθη τὸ ἕτερον ἐπίτασίν τε καὶ αὔξησιν ἐμφαίνειν παρὰ θάτερον, εἶτ’ οὖν τὸ ἰσχυρότεροι παρὰ τὸ εὐτονώτεροι, εἴτε τὸ εὐτονώτεροι παρὰ τὸ ἰσχυρότεροι· ἀλλ’ ὁμοειδές γε πάντως ἐπὶ τὸ σημαινόμενον ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων. ἔνθα δ’ αὔξησίς ἐστι, τοῦ εἴδους μένοντος, ἐνταῦθ’ οὐκ ἔστι διδασκαλία δυοῖν σημαινομένων. εὔδηλον δ’ ὅτι θατέρου γένους τοῦ πλήθους, ὃ πρὸς τὴν δύναμίν ἐστιν, οὐδὲ μέμνηται τὴν ἀρχὴν ὁ Ἐρασίστρατος, οὔτε οὖν κατὰ τοῦτο τὸ βιβλίον οὔτε ἐν τοῖς περὶ πυρετῶν.
rendering_1: [541] Does 'better-toned' signify something other than 'stronger', and did he teach us two signs of a moderate plethos, or, though he said two names, did he teach one sign? For my part I find no difference in what is signified, neither in respect of genus nor in respect of species nor in the more and the less, but I consider the same thing to be signified by each of the two. But if you wish, posit that the one indicates an intensification and increase in comparison with the other, whether 'stronger' in comparison with 'better-toned' or 'better-toned' in comparison with 'stronger'; yet what is signified from both is at all events of the same species. And where there is increase, the species remaining the same, there there is no teaching of two things signified. It is quite clear, moreover, that the other genus of plethos, that which is relative to the faculty, Erasistratus does not mention at all, neither in this book nor in the books On Fevers.
rendering_2: [541] Does 'more well-toned' (εὐτονώτεροι) signify something other than 'stronger' (ἰσχυρότεροι), so that he has taught us two signs of moderate plethos? Or did he state two names but only one sign? For my part, I find no difference in what is signified, neither in genus, nor in species, nor in the more and less; I hold that the same thing is signified by each. If you like, suppose that the one term displays an intensification and increase relative to the other, whether 'stronger' relative to 'more well-toned' or 'more well-toned' relative to 'stronger'. Even so, what is signified by both is certainly of the same species. And where there is an increase while the species remains, there is no teaching of two things signified. It is quite clear that Erasistratus does not even mention at all the other genus of plethos, the one that is relative to the capacity (δύναμις), neither in this book nor in his works on fevers.

greek: ὅσον μὲν γὰρ ἐπὶ τῇ προχείρῳ φαντασίᾳ, τὸ μὲν σκληρὸν καὶ ἀντίτυπον καὶ πυκνὸν ἑαυτὸ συνέχειν λέγοιτο, τὸ δ’ ἀραιόν τε ﻿ [528] καὶ μαλακὸν καὶ ὑπεῖκον ἑτέρου δεῖσθαι τοῦ συνέξοντος. οὐ μόνον δὲ οὐδεμίαν ἀπόδειξιν εἰπόντες οἱ ἄνδρες ἀξιοῦσι πιστεύεσθαι τὴν ὑπόθεσιν αὐτῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς ἑαυτὴν ὑποτιθέμενοι μαχομένην οὐκ ἔτι αἰσθάνονται. τὰ γὰρ ἁπάντων λεπτομερέστερα καὶ μαλακώτερα καὶ εἰκτικώτερα, τὸ πῦρ καὶ ἀέρα, ταῦτ’ αἴτια τῇ γῇ τῆς σκληρότητός τε καὶ ἀντιτυπίας εἶναί φασιν, ὡς ἐνδεχόμενον ἕτερον ἑτέρῳ τινὶ μεταδοῦναι δυνάμεως, ἢ φύσεως, ἢ ἐνεργείας, ἢ ποιότητος, ἧς οὐ μετείληφεν αὐτό. καὶ γὰρ αὖ καὶ φαίνεται σαφῶς οὐ μόνον οὐδὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς συνεχόμενον, ἀλλὰ καὶ διαλυόμενα πάντα. πρὸς μὲν δὴ τὴν τῶν Στωϊκῶν ὑπόθεσιν ἑτέρωθι λέλεκται διὰ πλειόνων· ἐπὶ δὲ τοὺς Ἡροφιλείους ἐπάνειμι, καὶ πρὸς τούτους ἀρκέσει μοι κατά γε τὸ παρὸν εἰπεῖν, ὡς προστάτης αὐτῶν ἐναντιώτατα πέπονθεν, ἀπορῶν μὲν ἐν παμπόλλοις ἀποδείξεις προχείρους ἔχουσιν, ἀποφαινόμενος δὲ ἐν ἄλλοις, ὧν αἵ τ’ ἀποδείξεις ἀδύνατοι ἥ θ’ ὑπόθεσις ψευδής.
rendering_1: For, so far as the ready appearance goes, what is hard and resistant and dense would be said to hold itself together, while what is rare [528] and soft and yielding would be said to need something else to hold it together. And not only do these men, having stated no demonstration, think it right that their hypothesis be believed, but they also no longer perceive that in positing it they make it conflict with itself. For the things that are finest in their particles and softest and most yielding of all, fire and air—these, they say, are the causes for earth of its hardness and resistance, as though it were possible for one thing to impart to another some power, or nature, or activity, or quality of which it itself has no share. And indeed, moreover, it is clearly evident not only that nothing is held together by fire, but also that all things are dissolved by it. Against the hypothesis of the Stoics, then, I have spoken at greater length elsewhere; but I return to the Herophileans, and against these it will suffice me, for the present at least, to say that their leader has been affected in the most contrary way: he is at a loss in very many matters that have ready demonstrations, yet pronounces confidently in others whose demonstrations are impossible and whose hypothesis is false.
rendering_2: For so far as the immediate impression goes, what is hard, resistant and dense might be said to hold itself together, and what is rare [528] and soft and yielding to need something else to hold it together. Yet not only do these men, having stated no demonstration at all, expect their hypothesis to be believed, but they also fail to notice that the hypothesis they posit is in conflict with itself. For the things that are of all the finest in their parts, the softest and the most yielding, namely fire and air, these, they say, are the causes to earth of its hardness and resistance, as though it were possible for one thing to impart to some other thing a faculty, or a nature, or an activity, or a quality in which it does not itself partake. And indeed it is, moreover, plainly seen not only that nothing is held together by fire, but that all things are dissolved by it. Against the hypothesis of the Stoics, then, the case has been argued at greater length elsewhere; I return to the Herophileans, and against them it will suffice me, for the present at least, to say that their leader has fared in the most contrary way: he professes perplexity in a great many matters that have ready demonstrations, but makes positive declarations in others whose demonstrations are impossible and whose hypothesis is false.

greek: ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν ἐν τῇ διαιρέσει τῶν λόγων ﻿ [543] ἐλλιπὲς οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ μόνον Ἐρασιστράτῳ σύνηθες, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατ’ ἄλλα συντάγματα σχεδὸν ἅπαντα. Τὸ δ’ οὖν εἰρημένον, ὁποῖόν ποτ’ ἂν ᾖ, πάλιν ἐπισκεψώμεθα. πληρουμένων τῶν ἀγγείων μετρίως, ἑαυτῶν εὐτονώτεροι φαίνονται. πότερον ὦ Ἐρασίστρατε κᾄν μηδὲ συναύξηται τῷ πλήθει τοῦ αἵματος ἡ ῥώμη τοῦ σώματος, ἢ καὶ αὐτῆς συναυξανομένης; ἐγὼ μὲν γὰρ ἀναγκαιότατον εἶναί φημι πρὸς τὴν εὐτονίαν τῆς ἐνεργείας καὶ τὴν ῥώμην τῆς δυνάμεως αὐξάνεσθαι. καὶ οὕτως δὲ, εἰ τῇ τοῦ αἵματος αὐξήσει μόνον, τῆς δυνάμεως τὰς ἐνεργείας ἰσχυροτέρας γένεσθαι ἡγῇ, τοῦ Ἀσκληπιάδου μᾶλλον ἀνατρέπειν δόξειας τὰς δυνάμεις. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐκεῖνος ἀπλῶς οὑτωσί φησιν, ᾧ πλέον αἷμα, πάντως τοῦτον εὐτονώτερον ὑπάρχειν, ᾧ δὲ ἔλαττον, ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀτονώτερον, ἀλλ’ εὑρήσεις τινὰς εἰπεῖν διορισμοὺς, ὁμολογοῦντας τοῖς φαινομένοις, καίτοι οὐδεμίαν ἡγούμενον ἐν ἡμῖν εἶναι δύναμιν οὔτε ψυχικὴν οὔτε ζωτικήν.
rendering_1: But this deficiency in the division of the arguments [543] is habitual to Erasistratus not only in this work but also in almost all his other treatises. Let us, then, examine again the statement itself, whatever it may be. "When the vessels are moderately filled, people appear in better tone than they themselves were." Is this so, Erasistratus, even if the strength of the body does not increase together with the quantity of the blood, or only when it too increases along with it? For my part, I say that for the good tone of the activity it is most necessary that the strength of the faculty also be increased. And so, if you believe that the activities of the faculty become stronger through the increase of the blood alone, you would seem to overturn the faculties more than Asclepiades does. For not even he says, in this simple way, that whoever has more blood is in every case in better tone, and whoever has less is of necessity in poorer tone; rather, you will find him stating certain qualifying distinctions that agree with the phenomena, even though he holds that there is no faculty in us, either psychic or vital.
rendering_2: But deficiency in the division of the arguments [543] is habitual with Erasistratus not only in this case but also in nearly all his other treatises. Let us, then, examine once more what has been said, whatever it may amount to. "When the vessels are moderately filled, people appear more vigorous than they were." Is this so, Erasistratus, even if the strength of the body is not increased together with the quantity of the blood, or only when it too is increased along with it? For I, for my part, say that it is most necessary, for the vigour of the activity, that the strength of the faculty also be increased. And so, if you think that the activities of the faculty become stronger by the increase of the blood alone, you would seem to overturn the faculties even more than Asclepiades does. For not even he says simply thus, that whoever has more blood is in every case more vigorous, and whoever has less is of necessity less vigorous; rather, you will find that he states certain distinctions which agree with the phenomena, even though he holds that there is no faculty in us at all, neither psychic nor vital.

greek: δῆλον δὲ ὡς εἰ καὶ παραλίποιμέν ποτε κατὰ τὰς τοιαύτας διαιρέσεις τὸ ἔκ τινων, ἢ ἐκ πάντων, αὐτὸ χρὴ προσυπακούειν τοὺς [537] ἀναγινώσκοντας τὸ βιβλίον, εἰδότας ὅτι κατὰ τοὺς τοιούτους ἅπαντας λόγους οἱ σύνδεσμοι οὐ διαζευκτικῶς, ἀλλὰ παραδιαζευκτικῶς εἰσιν. ἐκ μὲν δὴ τῶν εἰρημένων εὔδηλον, ὡς ὅστις βούλεται διαγνωστικὸς εἶναι πληθωρικοῦ μορίου, τοῦτον τῶν τε διοικουσῶν ἡμᾶς δυνάμεων ἐπιστήμην ἔχειν ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν, ἀνατομῆς τε καὶ φύσεως ἁπάντων ἀκριβῶς τῶν τοῦ ζώου μορίων· ἐκ τούτου γὰρ ὁρμώμενος ἴσως ἄν ποτε ἐξεύροιτο σημεῖα μορίου πληθωρικοῦ.
